newsitem.title: USA: Paramount wins lawsuit over Demi Moore photo.
newsitem.headline: Paramount wins lawsuit over Demi Moore photo.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent

A federal judge has thrown out a copyright infringement lawsuit against Paramount Pictures Corp. brought by Annie Leibovitz over a spoof of her famous nude magazine cover photo of pregnant actress Demi Moore.

U.S. District Judge Loretta Preska, in a ruling made public on Thursday, found that Paramount's ad for a "Naked Gun" film featuring comic actor Leslie Nielsen's face superimposed over a pregnant woman's body did not infringe on Leibovitz's copyright photo.

In her ruling, dated on Thursday, Preska found that Paramount's ad was a parody and a fair use of the copyright work, which appeared on the August 1991 cover of Vanity Fair magazine. She dismissed Leibovitz's argument that the ad was not a parody because it did not comment upon or criticise the Moore photograph.

"The Nielsen ad clearly takes satiric aim directly at the Moore photograph. From the outset, it was intended to make a mockery of an image that became a 'cultural icon'," Preska wrote. "In fact, without reference to the Moore photograph, the Nielsen ad simply is not very funny," she wrote.
The photo of Moore spurred controversy and public commentary when it was published, Preska wrote, noting that it was the best-selling single issue of the magazine at the time.
Tennison Schad, the New York lawyer representing Leibovitz, said he was shocked over the ruling.
"It is a black day for the creative community. I think it's wrong. We are weighing an appeal," Schad said.

The ad, which was used for the release of "Naked Gun: The Final Insult 33-1/3," bears Nielsen's smirking face over the body of an eight-months pregnant woman whose photo was subjected to some computer manipulation to duplicate Moore's skin tone and body configuration. Underneath the photo ran the legend "Due This March."
The ad was part of a "teaser campaign" designed to pique the public's interest in an upcoming movie.

Preska said that while the Moore photograph came to represent the view of pregnancy as a source of pride and a particular form of beauty, the Nielsen character in the film views pregnancy and fatherhood with "at best ambivalence, at worst stereotypical dread."
"This contradiction is part of what makes the Nielsen ad a parody," Preska wrote.
